# The Art of Being Lost: Finding Meaning in Uncertainty

There's something peculiar about modern life that I've been thinking about lately—how much energy we expend trying to avoid being lost. We have GPS coordinates for every address, career paths mapped out from childhood, self-help books promising to show us "the way," podcasts with titles like "Never Feel Uncertain Again." We've built an entire civilization around the premise that being lost is a failure state, something to be corrected as quickly as possible.

Yet I wonder if we've gotten this backwards.

I'm not talking about being lost in the sense of dangerous disorientation. I'm talking about the smaller, more existential variety. The kind that happens when you take a wrong turn in a city you've never visited before and end up discovering a café you would never have found otherwise. The kind that occurs when a career path crumbles and you realize you have no predetermined route forward. The kind that settles in when you reach a goal you've been chasing for years and discover it doesn't feel the way you thought it would.

We live in an age of increasing specialization and predetermined tracks. We're encouraged to "find our passion" as though it's something lying around waiting to be discovered, like car keys under a couch cushion. We're told to make a five-year plan, a ten-year plan, to have our lives organized by the time we're thirty. This narrative is everywhere, and it carries with it an implicit message: if you're not following a clear path, if you're uncertain, if you're lost—something has gone wrong.

But here's what I've noticed: some of the most interesting people I know are people who got lost and decided to stay lost long enough to actually look around.

There's a woman I met once who was a lawyer. She had the whole thing—the degree, the job at a respectable firm, the trajectory that looked exactly how it's supposed to. And then one day she realized that she'd been walking toward a destination for so long that she'd never actually asked herself if she wanted to go there. So she quit. She spent two years doing odd jobs, volunteering at a community center, reading philosophy, wandering through life without a plan. During that time, she discovered she wanted to work with youth in underserved communities. She didn't "find her passion" in some magical moment. She found it by allowing herself to be lost, by stepping off the path long enough to remember that she was allowed to choose her own direction.

I think about this differently than I did when I was younger. When I was in my early twenties, I believed that having a plan meant you were serious, that you were an adult making responsible choices. Not having a plan seemed reckless, indulgent, something people only did because they hadn't yet realized how the world actually worked. I was terrified of being lost because being lost seemed like a sign of failure, a sign that I'd made mistakes or wasn't good enough to succeed on the predetermined path.

What I didn't understand then is that the predetermined path is largely an illusion anyway. It's a story we tell ourselves, a narrative we overlay on top of life to make it feel more controllable than it actually is. Life is intrinsically uncertain. The most carefully laid plans can dissolve in an instant due to circumstances entirely beyond our control. We get sick. People we love disappoint us. Markets crash. Industries shift. Technologies emerge that render old skills obsolete. The world simply doesn't cooperate with our master plans the way we'd like it to.

So perhaps there's something to be said for getting lost on purpose.

I don't mean recklessly abandoning all planning or responsibility. I mean creating space for uncertainty, for exploration, for the possibility that you might discover something that wasn't on your original itinerary. I mean being willing to turn down paths that don't appear on the map.

There's a concept in Japanese aesthetics called "ma"—the space between things, the emptiness that gives form to the whole. Without the space between the notes, there would be no music, just noise. Without the white space on a page, there would be no clarity, just a wall of text. Without empty space in a composition, there's nowhere for the eye to rest, nowhere for the mind to wander.

I think humans need ma, too. We need empty space, unscheduled time, the freedom to wander. We need to not always know what comes next.

When I think about my own life, the moments I'd least like to erase are rarely the ones that went according to plan. They're the unexpected conversations with strangers on trains. The books I discovered by following a single reference down a rabbit hole of reading. The skills I picked up because I was curious about something, not because they fit neatly into a career trajectory. The relationships that formed because I was somewhere I didn't expect to be, doing something I hadn't planned to do.

The planned moments are fine. It's nice to accomplish things you've set out to accomplish. But they're not the ones that haunt you in the best way, that make you feel like you've actually *lived* something rather than just executed a plan.

There's also something about being lost that forces a kind of presence that planning doesn't. When you're following a predetermined path, you can be somewhat on autopilot. You know where you're supposed to be going, so you can let your mind wander to the next checkpoint. But when you're genuinely lost—when you don't know what comes next, when you have to actually pay attention to your surroundings and make decisions based on incomplete information—you're suddenly very present. You're alive to the moment in a way that a scheduled, mapped-out life rarely demands.

I've also come to understand that being lost is often where creativity lives. Every creative work, in some sense, requires venturing into territory that isn't fully mapped. When a writer sits down to write something new, they don't know exactly where the story will go. When a painter approaches a blank canvas, they're working with uncertainty. When a scientist designs an experiment, they're essentially saying, "I don't know what will happen, but I'm curious enough to find out." The edge of what we know is also the edge of what could be discovered.

This doesn't mean that planning is bad, or that structure is unnecessary. Certainly, we need enough order to function. But perhaps the problem in modern life is that we've swung too far toward total planning, toward the illusion of perfect control and predictability.

There's a reason that every successful creative person I've read about talks about the importance of play, of experimentation, of trying things without a predetermined outcome in mind. It's because without that space for lostness, without that willingness to explore without knowing where you'll end up, the work becomes sterile. It becomes about execution of a plan rather than about genuine creation.

I think about how children play before they're socialized into organized sports and structured activities. They just play. They follow their curiosity. They try things to see what happens. They're not trying to accomplish anything; they're just interested. And somehow, in that process, they're learning and growing and becoming more capable, but it's almost accidental—a byproduct of their attention rather than the goal.

Somewhere along the way, we tell them that this kind of unstructured play is a waste of time, that they should be using their time productively, working toward something. And maybe that's true to some degree. But I think we lose something important when we eliminate it entirely.

There's also the question of what it means to be "found." We talk about "finding yourself" or "finding your way" as though there's some stable, definable destination called the authentic self that you'll recognize once you arrive. But I'm not sure that's how it works. I think the self is more like a river than a location—it's constantly moving, changing, flowing. You're not trying to find a fixed point; you're learning to move with the current while also occasionally redirecting it.

Being lost is part of that process. It's not a deviation from the real journey; it's the real journey.

I think about the role that boredom and restlessness play in this, too. We've become very good at eliminating even moments of boredom. If we have a spare five minutes, we fill it with our phones. If we can't sleep, we listen to a podcast. If we're uncomfortable with silence, we play music. And I'm not judging this—I do it too. But there's something that happens when you're forced to just be with yourself, to sit with your own thoughts without distraction, that's valuable.

Some of my best ideas have come to me not while I was actively trying to solve a problem, but while I was bored, walking somewhere, with nothing particular on my mind. The space allows something to emerge.

I've also noticed that the fear of being lost often keeps people in situations that are slowly killing them. They stay in jobs that don't fulfill them because at least the path is clear. They stay in relationships that aren't working because the alternative—uncertainty—feels worse than the known unhappiness. They don't pursue interests that excite them because those interests don't fit into the plan.

In a way, staying in a bad situation because you're afraid of being lost is still being lost—it's just a more subtle kind of lostness, one that masquerades as having direction.

The people I know who seem most alive are the ones who've somehow made peace with uncertainty. They have plans, sure, but they hold them lightly. They're willing to change course if something more interesting appears. They're not waiting for permission to explore. They're not using the lack of a clear plan as an excuse to do nothing, but they're also not so attached to a predetermined path that they can't deviate when their interests or circumstances shift.

What I'm ultimately trying to say is this: being lost isn't a problem to be solved as quickly as possible. Sometimes being lost is exactly where you need to be. It's where you do your most interesting thinking. It's where you discover things about yourself you wouldn't have otherwise known. It's where genuine growth happens, as opposed to the mere execution of someone else's idea of what your life should look like.

The trick is learning to be lost without panicking. Learning to trust that not knowing where you're going doesn't necessarily mean you're going in the wrong direction. Learning that the most worthwhile destinations are often the ones you stumble upon by accident while looking for something else entirely.

So maybe the real skill we should be cultivating isn't the ability to always know exactly where we are on the map. Maybe it's the ability to get lost and stay calm enough to actually look around at where we've ended up. Maybe it's learning to follow our curiosity instead of our itinerary. Maybe it's understanding that the most meaningful lives are often the ones that look least like the plan.

We talk about finding ourselves as though it's a destination. But maybe we're not supposed to find ourselves. Maybe we're supposed to build ourselves, gradually, through all the small choices and detours and unexpected moments. And some of the most important building happens in the spaces between the plans, in the moments when we're genuinely lost and paying attention.
